newsitem.title: USA: EEP an option for new U.S. wheat crop - official.
newsitem.headline: EEP an option for new U.S. wheat crop - official.

text.p: A senior U.S. Agriculture Department official said Thursday that the government will probably not subsidize wheat exports in the current season, but held out the distinct possibility of subsidizing new crop wheat exports if necessary.

In an interview with Reuters, USDA's General Sales Manager Chris Goldthwait said given the tight ending stocks expected this fall, the department does not think that any additional sales would be gained by activating the Export Enhancement Program during the remaining months of this marketing year.

"Our focus for the moment is for the current season ... and we don't see the situation right now as warranting the use of the program," Goldthwait said. Goldthwait was attending the annual meeting of the National Grain and Feed Association, where he was scheduled to speak on Friday.
The USDA official, however, said the situation could change next year with a big U.S. wheat crop, surplus wheat supplies in Europe and Europe's willingness to subsidize its exports.

"What we can say now is that given the ability of the EU to behave very aggressively with export subsidies, we do need the tool so if they do that, and if we think we're losing market share, we'll have some way of responding," said Goldthwait.
Goldthwait questioned the value of EU using subsidies at this time, and said the EU is "wasting money."

He noted that the EU has reduced its subsidies in the last few weeks and attributed this to increased domestic usage, budgetary pressures, and the cumulative impact of forceful warnings from the United States and other countries that EU's use of subsidies could spark a price war.
Goldthwait said the EU could be limited next year in its use of export subsidies as a GATT ceiling begins to kick in, and he said there are reasons to "hope for continued restraint on their part."
Nevertheless, Goldthwait said Europe's "very large subsidy availability" has put the USDA on edge.
"We'd be more comfortable if the EU took a less aggressive stance," said Goldthwait.
